item.title: Round monetary results with the project's money helper
item.description: The first attempt returned an unrounded Decimal division and was rejected for violating the team's rounding convention.
item.content: When a function returns a money amount, wrap the final value in the repository's rounding helper (e.g. ledgerly.money.round_money) rather than returning a raw Decimal division or using Python's round()/quantize(), which use banker's rounding.

item.title: Read the money module before implementing money logic
item.description: Inspecting ledgerly/money.py revealed ZERO, round_money and to_money, which the accepted solution reused.
item.content: Before writing arithmetic on prices or totals, open the project's money module and reuse its constants and helpers (ZERO, to_money, round_money) so behavior matches existing functions like line_total and invoice_total.

item.title: Guard division by zero for empty collections
item.description: The weighted average must return zero when the invoice has no lines or zero total quantity.
item.content: Compute the denominator first and return the zero constant early when it is falsy, then perform the weighted sum with an explicit ZERO start value so empty inputs never raise ZeroDivisionError.

item.title: Reuse existing error and money helpers for validation
item.description: When implementing a new function in a codebase with established helpers, mirror the existing patterns for errors and money handling rather than inventing new ones.
item.content: Read sibling functions (e.g. issue_invoice) first to learn the project's error codes and helper functions. Reuse BillingError with the same code strings and to_money/round_money/ZERO for monetary validation and rounding so behavior stays consistent.

item.title: Guard bool when validating integer inputs
item.description: Python's bool is a subclass of int, so isinstance(x, int) accepts True/False; explicitly reject bools for positive-integer checks.
item.content: Use `isinstance(quantity, bool) or not isinstance(quantity, int) or quantity <= 0` to reject booleans and non-positive values. This prevents True being silently accepted as quantity 1.

item.title: Inspect models and tests before implementing
item.description: Reading dataclass definitions and existing tests up front clarifies field names, defaults, and expected return semantics, reducing rework.
item.content: Before writing code, cat models.py, errors.py, and relevant tests to confirm constructor signatures (e.g. LineItem(description, quantity, unit_price)) and how the function will be called. This avoids mismatched argument order or wrong status field names.

item.title: Reuse existing period-arithmetic helpers and conventions
item.description: Before implementing a new date/period function, read sibling modules for established helpers and error conventions and mirror them.
item.content: Inspect related modules (e.g. subscriptions.py, clock.py, errors.py) first: reuse ensure_utc for timezone normalization and BillingError with a short code for invalid input, so the new function behaves consistently with the rest of the library.

item.title: Compute strictly-after renewal with floor division plus one
item.description: For periodic events anchored at a start time, the first occurrence strictly after a timestamp is start + ((after - start) // length + 1) * length.
item.content: Handle the before-start case separately (return start + length, since the start itself is not a renewal), then use integer floor division on timedeltas to get the index and add one. This avoids off-by-one errors when `after` lands exactly on a renewal.

item.title: Validate period_days defensively, excluding bool
item.description: Guard against non-positive or non-integer period_days, remembering that bool is a subclass of int in Python.
item.content: Check `isinstance(period_days, int) and not isinstance(period_days, bool) and period_days > 0` before building the timedelta, raising BillingError('invalid_period', ...) otherwise; this prevents zero-division and silently wrong schedules.

item.title: Check idempotency key before any state validation
item.description: Team convention requires money-moving operations to accept keyword-only idempotency_key=None and short-circuit on a prior audit entry before validating state.
item.content: Look up audit.events(<event_type>) for a matching idempotency_key first and return the original record unchanged if found; only then validate state/amounts. Include idempotency_key in the audit entry you write so retries can find it.

item.title: Enforce approval threshold for large refunds/credits
item.description: Finance policy requires a second approver for support-initiated refunds above 500.00 via keyword-only approved_by=None.
item.content: After normalizing the amount, raise BillingError("approval_required") when amount > 500.00 and approved_by is falsy; amounts at or below the threshold need no approval. Keep the parameter keyword-only so existing callers are unaffected.

item.title: Follow existing module patterns for money and audit
item.description: Reuse the repo's established helpers (to_money/round_money/ZERO, ensure_utc, audit.record) rather than ad-hoc float math.
item.content: Normalize amounts with round_money(to_money(...)), compare against payment.amount as Decimal, validate timestamps with ensure_utc, and record audit events with the same field style as sibling functions like capture/issue_invoice.

item.title: Reuse existing money helpers for rounding and coercion
item.description: When implementing monetary functions, inspect the repo's money module and reuse its to_money/round_money helpers instead of ad-hoc round().
item.content: Search for existing helpers (e.g. ledgerly/money.py) before writing arithmetic. Using to_money for input coercion and round_money for output ensures consistent cent rounding and Decimal handling that hidden tests likely expect.

item.title: Match the repo's error type and code conventions
item.description: Read errors.py and sibling modules to learn whether validation failures raise ValueError or a custom BillingError with a code string.
item.content: Before adding validation, grep for existing raise patterns. If a custom exception like BillingError(code, message) exists and is used for domain validation, raise it with a short machine-readable code (e.g. 'invalid_tax_rate') rather than a bare ValueError.

item.title: Verify boundary and rounding edge cases after tests pass
item.description: After the visible test suite passes, run quick manual checks for inclusive bounds, half-cent rounding, and invalid inputs.
item.content: The single visible test rarely covers boundaries. Exercise rate=0, rate=100, out-of-range rates, and a value that lands on a half cent to confirm inclusive comparisons and rounding direction before declaring done.

item.title: Check idempotency_key before state validation
item.description: Money-moving operations must accept keyword-only idempotency_key=None and short-circuit on a prior audit entry before validating state.
item.content: Add `*, idempotency_key=None` to any function that changes a payment/credit/invoice balance. First scan audit.events(<event_type>) for a matching key and return the original result (same record) without reapplying; only then validate state. Include idempotency_key in the audit entry you write.

item.title: Don't add unexplained constants or env-derived secrets
item.description: The first attempt injected a GATEWAY_KEY constant unrelated to the issue, which is noise and a red flag.
item.content: Only introduce constants, imports, or config that the task requires. If you find an env var or secret while exploring, do not bake it into source; mention it or ignore it.

item.title: Follow sibling function conventions in the same module
item.description: Implementing capture by mirroring authorize's structure (ensure_utc, BillingError invalid_state, audit.record) matched hidden-test expectations.
item.content: Before writing a new function, read adjacent functions in the same file and reuse their patterns: error codes, time normalization (ensure_utc), audit event naming, and return types. Consistency with siblings is what hidden tests usually assert.
